title: Lithium-induced ECG modifications: navigating from acute coronary syndrome to Brugada syndrome
case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman with a 10-year history of bipolar disorder treated with lithium (1650 mg/day) and risperidone presented after a week of persistent symptoms that began as dry cough, sweats, and fever. She was referred to the emergency department after developing delirium and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, the temperature was 39°C, heart rate was irregular and tachycardic, blood pressure was 149/87 mm Hg, and there was tenderness in the right upper abdominal quadrant. Laboratory studies showed a normal white-cell count, C-reactive protein of 43.5 mg/dL, hyponatremia (129 mmol/L), corrected calcium 2.61 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 mmol/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L (baseline 48 µmol/L), positive urine culture for Escherichia coli, and a serum lithium concentration of 2.0 mmol/L (therapeutic range 0.8–1.2 mmol/L). An ECG on admission demonstrated atrial fibrillation with a wide QRS complex (160 ms) and ST-segment elevation in leads V1 and V2. A previous ECG from 2014 showed sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS and first-degree atrioventricular block. Abdominal CT with contrast confirmed pyelonephritis and ruled out cholecystitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute coronary syndrome was considered but deemed unlikely — “This alternative was however relatively unlikely considering the ST elevation limited to leads V1 and V2 without reciprocal changes.”  
2. Myocardial infarction was further excluded by biomarker assessment — “the result was only slightly elevated, without dynamic change (20 ng/L for ULN at 15 ng/L), possibly secondary to acute kidney injury.”  
3. Ischemic wall-motion abnormalities were excluded on imaging — “focused transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), which showed no wall-motion abnormality.”  
4. Sepsis and electrolyte disturbance were recognized contributors to arrhythmia — “AF and the other ECG modifications, were deemed multifactorial, with the involvement of sepsis, electrolyte imbalance and lithium intoxication.”  
5. Lithium intoxication was implicated in conduction and repolarization changes — “ECG pattern normalized after restoring normal values of blood lithium levels.”  
6. Brugada syndrome was ultimately diagnosed when characteristic ECG morphology persisted and was unmasked under sodium-channel blockade — “ECG obtained with the placement of leads V1 and V2 in the third intercostal spaces showed a typical Brugada type 1 pattern with coved ST-segment elevation of more than 2 mm in V1 and V2, followed by a negative T wave.”
